summary: Describes the general PANA framework, including its functional elements, a high-level call flow, and deployment environments. It gives background for understanding how the protocol is meant to be used. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5193 describes the shape of PANA, a protocol that lets a device authenticate itself before it uses an access network. It names the four parties involved, shows the messages they exchange, and explains the two kinds of network the design has to work in.

subtitle: The four pieces of a network access control system, and how a client gets authorised on it.

tldr.problem: A client that attaches to an access network has to prove who it is, and the network has to be told to let that client's traffic through. Existing mechanisms were tied to a particular link technology.
tldr.mechanism: PANA defines a new lower layer for EAP that runs over IP, and the document describes the four entities involved, the message flow between them, and the two deployment situations the design has to cover.
tldr.outcome: Nothing here is a protocol specification. The details are in RFC 5191, the requirements in RFC 4058, and the threat analysis in RFC 4016.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
PANA, the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access, is a link-layer agnostic network access authentication protocol that runs between a client seeking access to the network and a server on the network side. PANA defines a new Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) lower layer that uses IP between the protocol end points. The motivation and the requirements are described in RFC 4058, and the protocol details in RFC 5191.

After a successful PANA authentication, per-packet security can be achieved by physical security, link-layer ciphering, or IPsec. The PANA server implementation may or may not sit on the same node as the entity that enforces per-packet access control; when they are separate, a protocol such as the Access Node Control Protocol may carry information between the two nodes.

PANA is meant for any access network regardless of the underlying security. The network might be physically secured, or secured by cryptographic means after the client has been authenticated. While a PANA deployment must implement behaviour that ensures the integrity of PANA messages when the EAP method produces an MSK, it is not mandatory to support network security at the link layer or the network layer. The document defines the general framework for describing how the PANA and other network access authentication elements interact, in particular for the two basic types of deployment environment.
sections.plainLanguage: PANA exists so that a device can be checked before it is allowed to send traffic on an access network, without the check depending on the kind of link the device is plugged into. The check itself uses EAP, the framework that lets different authentication methods plug in, and PANA supplies the missing piece: a way to carry EAP over IP.

sections.title: The Four Functional Entities
sections.content:
PANA is an EAP lower layer that carries EAP authentication methods, encapsulated inside EAP, between a client node and a server in the access network. It enables the authentication process between the two entities, but it is only part of an overall AAA and access control framework, which is made up of four functional entities.

The PANA Client (PaC) is the client implementation of PANA, residing on the node requesting network access. A PaC can be an end host such as a laptop, PDA, cell phone or desktop PC, or a router connected by a wired or wireless interface. It requests network access and takes part in the authentication process using PANA.

The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) is the server implementation. It interfaces with the PaCs to authenticate and authorize them for the network access service, and it consults an authentication server to verify the credentials and rights of the PaC. If the authentication server is on the same node, an API is enough; when they are separated, which is the common case in public access networks, a protocol must run between them, and AAA protocols such as RADIUS or Diameter are commonly used. The PAA is also responsible for updating the access control state, that is the filters, as authorization state is created and deleted, and it communicates the updated state to the Enforcement Points. The PAA typically resides on a node called a NAS, for example a BRAS in DSL networks or a PDSN in 3GPP2 networks, and may be one or more IP hops from the PaCs.

The Authentication Server (AS) verifies the credentials of a PaC. It receives requests from the PAA on behalf of the PaCs and responds with the result of the verification together with the authorization parameters, such as allowed bandwidth and IP configuration. It is the server that terminates the EAP and the EAP methods, and it might be hosted on the same node as the PAA, on a dedicated node in the access network, or on a central server somewhere in the Internet.

The Enforcement Point (EP) allows data traffic from authorized clients and prevents access by others. It learns the attributes of the authorized clients from the PAA and uses non-cryptographic or cryptographic filters to allow and discard packets, at the link layer or the IP layer. When cryptographic access control is used, a secure association protocol must run between the PaC and the EP; afterwards, link or network layer per-packet security such as TKIP or IPsec ESP gives integrity protection, data origin authentication, replay protection and optionally confidentiality. The EP sits between the access network and the accessed network, and it is recommended but not mandated that it be on the path between the PaC and the PAA, so that unauthorized packets are dropped before they reach any other client, for example by hosting the EP on the switch directly connected to the clients.

Some of these entities may be colocated. In DSL networks the PAA and the EP are often on the same BRAS, where a simple API suffices between them. In small enterprise deployments the PAA and the AS may be hosted on the same access router, which removes the need for a protocol between them. Which entities are colocated and where they sit are deployment decisions outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Four roles. The client asks for access. The authentication agent on the network side handles that request and asks a separate server to check the credentials. The enforcement point is the door that actually lets traffic through, and it learns which client to let in from the authentication agent. Which of these run on the same box is a choice each deployment makes.

sections.title: Call Flow
sections.content:
The EP on the access network allows general data traffic from any authorized PaC, but only a limited type of traffic, such as PANA, DHCP and router discovery, for unauthorized PaCs. That gives a newly attached client the minimum access service it needs to run PANA and become authorized.

The PaC configures an IP address, dynamically or statically, before running PANA. After a successful authentication, depending on the deployment, it may need to reconfigure its address or configure additional addresses. For example, a link-local IPv6 address may be used for PANA and the PaC may then be allowed to configure additional global IPv6 addresses, or a PaC may be limited to an IPv4 link-local address during PANA and allowed to reconfigure its interface with a non-link-local IPv4 address afterwards. General-purpose applications cannot use the interface until PANA succeeds and the appropriate address configuration has taken place.

An initially unauthorized PaC starts PANA authentication by discovering the PAA, followed by the EAP exchange over PANA, and the PAA interacts with the AS during that process. When it receives the authentication and authorization result from the AS, the PAA tells the PaC the result of its network access request.

If the PaC is authorized, the PAA also sends the PaC-specific attributes, such as an IP address and cryptographic keys, to the EP using another protocol. The EP uses this information to change its filters so that data traffic to and from the PaC passes through. Where cryptographic access control must be enabled after PANA, a secure association protocol runs between the PaC and the EP, and the dynamic parameters it needs, such as endpoint identity and shared secret, are derived from the successful PANA authentication; these parameters authenticate the PaC to the EP and the EP to the PaC as part of creating the security association. The exchange produces the security associations that enable cryptographic data traffic protection. That protection adds per-packet overhead, but only between the PaC and the EP, and does not affect communications beyond the EP. Finally, the filters installed at the EP let general purpose data traffic flow between the PaC and the intranet or the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The sequence is: the client finds the authentication agent and runs the EAP exchange through it. The agent asks the authentication server whether the client is allowed in, tells the client the answer, and separately tells the enforcement point which client to let through and with what address and keys. If the network wants each packet encrypted, a further exchange between the client and the enforcement point sets that up using keys from the PANA result.

sections.title: Deployment Environments
sections.content:
PANA can be used in any network environment, whether a lower-layer secure channel already exists between the PaC and the EP before PANA runs or one has to be enabled after a successful authentication.

In the first kind, a secure channel is available before PANA runs. Such a network has protection against spoofing and eavesdropping, but user authentication and authorization is still required for network connectivity. One example is a DSL network where lower-layer security comes from physical means: protecting the network wiring ensures that in practice only one client can send and receive IP packets on the link. Another is a cdma2000 network where lower-layer security comes from cryptographic protection; by the time the client asks for network-layer services it is already authenticated and authorized for the radio channel, and link-layer ciphering is enabled. The presence of a secure channel before the PANA exchange removes the need for a secure association protocol afterwards, the PANA session can be tied to the channel it was carried over, and the choice of EAP method depends on the security present while PANA runs.

In the second kind, the secure channel is created after PANA runs. There is no lower-layer protection beforehand, so PANA authentication happens on a channel that is open to eavesdropping and spoofing. The choice of EAP method must be resilient to the attacks possible in such an environment, and the method must be able to create the cryptographic keys the later secure association protocol will use. Whether to use link-layer or network-layer per-packet security is a deployment decision outside the scope of the document, and that decision also dictates the choice of secure association protocol: link-layer protection means a link-layer specific protocol, while IP-layer protection means IKE and per-packet security from IPsec AH or ESP regardless of the underlying link-layer technology.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two situations. In one, the link is already trustworthy, for instance because the wiring is physically protected or because the radio link is already encrypted, so PANA only has to check the user's identity. In the other, the link is open, so the authentication method has to survive an eavesdropper, and once the client is authenticated a further handshake sets up encryption for each packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security is discussed throughout the document. For protocol-specific security considerations the reader is referred to RFC 4016, the PANA threat analysis and security requirements, and to RFC 5191, the protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework itself says little about threats. It points to the threat analysis document and to the protocol specification for that part of the story.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FUNCTIONAL ENTITIES OF THE PANA MODEL

items.title: PaC
items.text: The client on the node asking for access. It runs PANA and may be a laptop, phone, router or similar device.

items.title: PAA
items.text: The authentication agent. It talks to the clients, consults the authentication server, and updates the filters at the enforcement points.

items.title: AS
items.text: The authentication server. It verifies credentials, returns the authorization parameters, and terminates EAP.

items.title: EP
items.text: The enforcement point. It applies filters at the link or IP layer to let authorized traffic through and drop the rest.
